claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is an as-cast, homogeneous, metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution.
Thermal exposure can drive a metastable high-entropy-alloy solid solution to decompose.
The decomposition is thermodynamically driven and thermally activated.
During thermal aging, Mg segregates from the solid solution.
Segregated Mg precipitates as Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially develop along grain boundaries.
With continued thermal exposure, initially fine intermetallic precipitates coarsen and may form interconnected paths.
The length scale of phase decomposition depends on alloy composition and annealing temperature.
Low volume fractions of finely dispersed, isolated intermetallics may have negligible effects on corrosion and oxidation resistance.
An interconnected intermetallic network creates localized galvanic couples.
An interconnected grain-boundary intermetallic network provides rapid or enhanced oxygen-diffusion pathways.
Localized galvanic coupling caused by interconnected intermetallics accelerates corrosion.
Enhanced oxygen transport along interconnected intermetallic paths accelerates high-temperature oxidation.
Thermally aged specimens will contain measurable quantities of Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the as-cast state.
Once the precipitates become coarsened and interconnected, aged specimens will exhibit higher corrosion rates or lower breakdown potentials than the as-cast baseline.
Once the precipitates become coarsened and interconnected, aged specimens will develop thicker or less protective oxide scales than the as-cast baseline.
The detrimental transition occurs beyond a percolation or connectivity threshold for the intermetallic phase.
The critical intermetallic volume fraction, distribution, and connectivity may vary with small compositional differences.
